sources.title: Tessl AI Native Dev ep 124: Dexter Horthy, Why We Stopped Trusting AI to Write the Plan
sources.note: Full publisher transcript (RSS). Dex = SPEAKER_01; hosts SPEAKER_03 (Guy Podjarny) and SPEAKER_00 (Simon Maple, ads). Whole file read.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we ran this for like four or five months before we realized
cards.claim: Reviewing the plan instead of the code ('trust the plan, skip the code') ran 4-5 months at HumanLayer and left the codebase unusable, with each change regressing something else.
cards.evidence_detail: Own team's 4-5 month experiment; no numbers beyond duration.
cards.landing: Reinforces keeping code review per PR and the Opus reviewer; argues against plan-only review.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we literally rebuilt the whole product from scratch
cards.claim: After the experiment HumanLayer rebuilt the product from scratch, and the cofounder hand-typed the data architecture for the first two weeks.
cards.landing: Human-owned data architecture decided early; relevant to phase-0 design decisions.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the plans contained all of the code that was gonna be written
cards.claim: Plans written as inline diffs made reviewers read the same code twice (plan then implementation drift), so plan review did not save review effort.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed at HumanLayer and at 50-developer client teams.
cards.landing: Plan @ sha PR body: keep plans at design level, not inline code.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: let the model own the system architecture too
cards.claim: Letting the model own architecture produced a six-service system (Rust, Golang daemon, Unix sockets, MCP, SQLite) of needless complexity; humans must own architecture decisions.
cards.landing: Architecture/schema decisions stay human-set in the plan phase.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: to debug code, you need to be like much smarter than you were
cards.claim: Citing the Kernighan/Knuth-style principle, he argues systems must stay simpler than peak intelligence because models write clever code they cannot debug (and cites Steve Yegge's recent retraction).
cards.landing: Simplicity bias in reviewer rubric.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: in July of 2025, plan file was a reliable way to get a model to work longer
cards.claim: Changed position: the main value of a plan file in mid-2025 was making a model work longer and resumable (compaction of intent), a leverage that has shifted with better models.
cards.landing: Plan file as cold-resume artifact (P1 trial).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: around a hundred thousand tokens. If you went over a hundred thousand tokens
cards.claim: The 'dumb zone' was about 100k tokens in July 2025; the number is higher now, though he still thinks context engineering and less context always give better results.
cards.evidence_detail: Change of number: 100k then, higher now, no new figure given.
cards.landing: Supports one-phase-per-session; do not hard-code a threshold.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you will get better quality if you use less context
cards.claim: Context engineering is a first principle that will stay true while transformer LLMs are used, unchanged since 18 months ago.
cards.landing: Justifies trimming CLAUDE.md.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't have too many PRs, you have too many bad PRs
cards.claim: Drowning in PRs is a symptom of people turning off their brains while coding; planning/alignment up front makes PRs easy to review.
cards.landing: Plan-before-build reduces review cost.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think about this in terms of expected pain.
cards.claim: Choose how much to plan by expected pain (chance of rework times cost of rework): align on the database schema, do not argue about button colour.
cards.landing: Plan-depth rule: heavier planning only for schema/migration/money work.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Don't YOLO a two-sentence prompt and not read the code
cards.claim: A two-sentence prompt has about a 50% chance of rework; never send unread code of that kind to another person to review.
cards.landing: Author self-review before PR.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We have a bunch of different planning workflows.
cards.claim: HumanLayer keeps several planning workflows (design doc then ship; design plus ordering; a 3-4 stage PRD flow) chosen by feature size, each slicing off bad outcomes.
cards.landing: Tiered planning workflows in a reusable workflow library.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: relentlessly interview the user
cards.claim: Intent is best captured by rambling by voice for 60 seconds, then having the model interview the user relentlessly (grill-me style) down the decision tree.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; cites popularity of Matt Pocock's grill-me skill.
cards.landing: A grill-me skill in the skill packages.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we call it like back pressure
cards.claim: A good spec plus backpressure (feedback the model can get without a human) lets agents work two hours unattended and parallelise.
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts as verifier inputs.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm not reading any of that code.
cards.claim: Not reading code is fine for prototypes that prove what is possible (evolutionary subagent hill-climbing on 45 evals); then distil to a spec and reimplement cleanly.
cards.landing: Throwaway prototype lane distinct from shipped code.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it didn't actually get that much better at writing code that is maintainable
cards.claim: Frontier models improved at computer use and other domains but not at writing maintainable code; waiting for the next model is not a plan.
cards.evidence_detail: Reports of 'every good builder he knows'.
cards.landing: Keep human/Opus review of maintainability.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: There's no fast oracle for software maintainability.
cards.claim: Maintainability lacks a fast oracle (you learn two months later), so RL cannot train it and models improve slowly at it.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning; credited partly to riffing with Addy Osmani.
cards.landing: Do not expect automated verifiers to judge maintainability; keep human review.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think GPT-5.5 in May got a 14.8%.
cards.claim: SlopCodeBench (not his; a University of Wisconsin lab, Dex helping with runs): sequential feature tasks inheriting the codebase; GPT-5.5 scored 14.8% in May and Astra 16.3% on the first run.
cards.landing: Benchmark baseline for maintaining a codebase over time; slow improvement.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a hundred bullet points into their claude MD, most of them don't get followed
cards.claim: CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md accumulating many always/never bullets means most are not followed because it is too much context; split opinions into skills.
cards.landing: Trim CLAUDE.md and move rules into skills.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every morning we wake up to five pull requests
cards.claim: HumanLayer runs four or five nightly cron/GitHub Action agents (same harness, different user message) with deterministic detectors (React Doctor, lint) that open PRs improving the codebase along one dimension.
cards.landing: Nightly cleanup workflows driven by deterministic detectors.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more opinions you have, the more clever you have to be
cards.claim: Many codified opinions force clever context engineering: splitting into skills, parallelising and orchestrating multiple agents.
cards.landing: Skill packaging of conventions.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: big design up front is always gonna lose to iterate fast
cards.claim: Building a software factory by throwing everything out and designing from scratch loses to getting 1% better every day or week.
cards.landing: Incremental harness change, not a big-bang rebuild.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it degrades every future piece of work that goes through that factory
cards.claim: Unlike a car factory, bad output in a software factory degrades all later work because the model copies bad patterns; stop the bleeding before scaling.
cards.landing: Gate bad patterns at merge; humans in the loop.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: analyzing the session traces of everyone on your team
cards.claim: Siphon PR review comments and session traces into factory improvements (skills, review skill) by finding where people get frustrated; if not improving you are getting worse.
cards.landing: Mining transcripts for corrections feeds the knowledge store.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: from kind of building the car to building the factory
cards.claim: Shift from caring about each output to the velocity of the system that makes outputs, spending less time on individual code review over time.
cards.landing: Invest in reusable workflows.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there will probably always be alpha in reviewing something
cards.claim: Humans will always have to review something (now code, later something else), or output matches everyone else's median; a founder's remark that he adopts.
cards.evidence_detail: Dinner poll: all AI-written, about half still read code; 1-2 years to stop reviewing.
cards.landing: Keep human review as a deliberate lane.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: do not mortgage your code base for the future
cards.claim: Advice to large enterprises: move fast without giving up control or taste; accept a ~1% chance of missing upside.
cards.landing: Risk posture for a money-handling system.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: understanding the problem better than anyone else
cards.claim: The durable moat is understanding the customer problem and knowing what to ask the factory for, which lets you context-engineer better than competitors.
cards.landing: Owner domain knowledge captured in the store.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: let the model context engineer the human
cards.claim: Build faster-than-reading-code review aids (50-80% faster) so the model explains what it did to the human efficiently, and brain-drains the human of tastes quickly.
cards.landing: Six-question closing message and one-page owner view are this.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the entire software factory stack will decompose into good interfaces
cards.claim: Predicts factory stacks will become open, portable components like Kubernetes, and advises against building on a single vendor's walled-garden stack.
cards.landing: Keep harness vendor-portable.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: three copies, press hard
cards.claim: Taste rules such as duplicating three lines instead of abstracting are hard to put in a model and must be written as explicit opinions.
cards.landing: Short named taste rules in skills.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there's just slop everywhere right now
cards.claim: Chose a real-time sync database early; early architecture decisions cascade, and he reads code to catch slop patterns models create unattended.
cards.landing: Early decisions human-owned.

gaps: Transcript has no speaker names; Dex identified as SPEAKER_01 by content.
Quotes are from an automatic publisher transcript and may include mishearings (e.g. 'Fable', 'Astra', 'Jev' for model/product names).
Some card quotes are lightly condensed from the transcript text and may not be exact verbatim.

new_sources.title: SlopCodeBench (University of Wisconsin lab)
new_sources.why: Dex cites it as the maintainability benchmark; 14.8% and 16.3% figures.

new_sources.title: Steve Yegge's recent retraction about a model-built system it could not debug
new_sources.why: Dex cites it as a real-world counterexample to lights-off development.
